messages.author: 71221bf487359d78
messages.subject: OLS/ LMMs
parts:
Hi,

I'm working through a userGWAS and am having somewhat of a hard time determining the specifications for the sumstats function. My first question is should we be specifying OLS=T even if the model is an LMM? Or does the OLS specification just refer to any linear, continuous GWAS? And relatedly how much of an issue are LMMs with GSEM? I know BOLT-LMM employs the leave-one-chromosome-out method, but I'm not totally sure if the following text is saying MLMe is ok but MLMi (in Yang's terms) isn't? And if we should not be using BOLT-LMM generated sumstats with GSEM is there a reference for that?

"Another issue is the use of "linear mixed models" (LMM) in GWAS. These models are used to guard against populations stratification, and cryptic relatedness between study participants. The pitfalls of, and opportunities afforded by, these models are discussed by Yang et al (2014). These models guard against cryptic relatedness in a sample by determining the relationship between all pairs of subjects in a study, and fitting a random effect based on this information. Important for you to know is that there are two types of mixed models. The first type, which Yang et al. call "MLMi," uses all SNPs in determining the relationship between subjects, including the SNP that is entered as a fixed effect into the model. This type of mixed model is best considered incompatible with GenomicSEM and LD score regression in general. The second type of mixed model, which Yang et al. call "MLMe," determines cryptic relatedness between pairs of participants based on all chromosomes but the one on which the SNP considered as a fixed effect is located. This leads to a downward biased estimate of heritability in LD score regression and therefore also in GenomicSEM."

Thanks!
Claire

messages.author: d6d83e22ef3ba9f1
messages.subject: Re: OLS/ LMMs
parts:
Hi Claire, 

Great question! If it was BOLT-LMM for a continuous phenotype than the correct specification would be OLS=T. I would say it is a little unclear how best to deal with BOLT-LMM results in Genomic SEM at the moment, but I can make some general suggestions based on what we’ve observed. 

1. If you go to the referenced Yang et al. (2014) paper "Advantages and pitfalls in the application of mixed-model association methods" they examine the relationship between the chi-square from traditional linear regression and two different types of mixed model approaches: MLMe and MLMi. In Figure 1 of this paper you can see that MLMi leads to a clear deflation in the chi-square statistic relative to linear regression, and will consequently result in a deflation in the heritability estimate obtained from LDSC and is therefore not appropriate for LDSC. Not super relevant because most packages developed recently uses MLMe, including SAIGE and BOLT-LMM. The relationship between the linear regression and MLMe is not exactly 1, but we've generally found for traits with h2 < 50% and participant sample sizes < 400k that BOLT-LMM and traditional linear regression LDSC results are very similar when comparing estimates obtained from the same participant samples and phenotypes. So when running a model without individual SNP effects using the usermodel function, estimates from MLMe (and consequently BOLT-LMM) seem to be fine to use in Genomic SEM. 

2. While the heritability estimate should be very consistent between MLMe and traditional linear models, Loh et al. (2018) find in a paper titled “Mixed-model association for biobank-scale datasets,” that it is the univariate LDSC intercept in BOLT-LMM that is the most difficult to interpret as it will “rise above 1 with increasing sample size and heritability.” This LDSC univariate intercept is used in the sampling covariance matrix for the multivariate GWAS to account for confounding, and so BOLT-LMM estimates will produce an inflated LDSC intercept and consequently conservative multivariate GWAS estimates. Since BOLT-LMM controls for sample structure that would otherwise be captured by the LDSC univariate intercept, for BOLT-LMM traits I would say it is most sensible to set the LDSC intercept to 1. For right now, this can be achieved by manually setting the diagonals of the intercept matrix (the third part of the LSC output named I) for the BOLT-LMM traits to 1. 

Best, 

  Andrew

parts:

My feeling is no, especially if the meta-analysis is a mix of continuous and binary cohorts, OLS would be F. But perhaps even if the meta-analysis is all continuous cohorts it would still be OLS=F because METAL isn't performing a linear regression per say but is calculating an overall z-statistic and p-value from a weighted sum of the individual statistics?

Claire

messages.author: 3b39745f73eec779
messages.subject: Re: OLS/ LMMs
parts:
Hi Claire,

So a meta-analysis of OLS GWAS should be OLS=T (because asymptotically and under some conditions the meta-analysis is equal to a grouped analysis of the data), a mix is harder to rationalise. 

OLS =F ls only there tell GenopmicSEM (log)odds to the liability scale. Its in retrospect a bad name for the argument. However I feel we're to deep into this whole GenomicSEM thing to change it....

at the time the only GWAS we considered were GWAS (or meta's) that used OLS/LMM (with caveats for LMM) as an estimator or logistic regression.

if you have a Z, you need OLS =T I think (though will need to use approximate N if the meta is a mix of binary and continuous).

Michel

Hi Claire, 

Just a note that the correct arguments for binary and continuous traits meta-analyzed in METAL actually came up for someone else and I took a look at different combinations of arguments for the sumstats function and found that OLS = T produces p-values that exactly mirror that in the original summary statistics file. For this particular set of summary statistics there was a sample size column that the function used, so as Michel notes the one difficulty may be coming up with the appropriate N to provide if it isn't in the summary stats file. 

-Andrew

messages.author: d6d83e22ef3ba9f1
messages.subject: Re: OLS/ LMMs
parts:
Thanks for bringing this up! I actually want to walk back my initial comment of using the concordance between the output of sumstats and original p-values as a litmus test for whether arguments for sumstats are correctly specified. In reality, I think you are seeing perfect concordance (versus what I suspect are correlations of .98 or greater) when specifying se.logit = F and OLS = T because of rounding, or at least that has been my experience. So as Michel noted, the real reason for using OLS = T for a meta-analysis of binary and continuous traits is that this theoretically should be the right option when the output is a Z-statistic. 

So to clarify, the arguments passed to sumstats really should be about what columns are in the summary statistics files and how those summary statistics were produced. So if you have binary traits with summary statistics files that include logistic betas or OR then you should not be setting OLS = T, and whether se.logit = F or T should be determined based on whether the SE is for the OR or on a logistic scale. Similarly, you should be using pop and samp prev for these traits for the ldsc function. Apologies for the confusion there and let us know if you have any questions.

Hi Claire, 

Great question! If it was BOLT-LMM for a continuous phenotype than the correct specification would be OLS=T. I would say it is a little unclear how best to deal with BOLT-LMM results in Genomic SEM at the moment, but I can make some general suggestions based on what we’ve observed. 

1. If you go to the referenced Yang et al. (2014) paper "Advantages and pitfalls in the application of mixed-model association methods" they examine the relationship between the chi-square from traditional linear regression and two different types of mixed model approaches: MLMe and MLMi. In Figure 1 of this paper you can see that MLMi leads to a clear deflation in the chi-square statistic relative to linear regression, and will consequently result in a deflation in the heritability estimate obtained from LDSC and is therefore not appropriate for LDSC. Not super relevant because most packages developed recently uses MLMe, including SAIGE and BOLT-LMM. The relationship between the linear regression and MLMe is not exactly 1, but we've generally found for traits with h2 < 50% and participant sample sizes < 400k that BOLT-LMM and traditional linear regression LDSC results are very similar when comparing estimates obtained from the same participant samples and phenotypes. So when running a model without individual SNP effects using the usermodel function, estimates from MLMe (and consequently BOLT-LMM) seem to be fine to use in Genomic SEM. 

2. While the heritability estimate should be very consistent between MLMe and traditional linear models, Loh et al. (2018) find in a paper titled “Mixed-model association for biobank-scale datasets,” that it is the univariate LDSC intercept in BOLT-LMM that is the most difficult to interpret as it will “rise above 1 with increasing sample size and heritability.” This LDSC univariate intercept is used in the sampling covariance matrix for the multivariate GWAS to account for confounding, and so BOLT-LMM estimates will produce an inflated LDSC intercept and consequently conservative multivariate GWAS estimates. Since BOLT-LMM controls for sample structure that would otherwise be captured by the LDSC univariate intercept, for BOLT-LMM traits I would say it is most sensible to set the LDSC intercept to 1. For right now, this can be achieved by manually setting the diagonals of the intercept matrix (the third part of the LSC output named I) for the BOLT-LMM traits to 1. 

Best, 

  Andrew

Thanks for bringing this up! I actually want to walk back my initial comment of using the concordance between the output of sumstats and original p-values as a litmus test for whether arguments for sumstats are correctly specified. In reality, I think you are seeing perfect concordance (versus what I suspect are correlations of .98 or greater) when specifying se.logit = F and OLS = T because of rounding, or at least that has been my experience. So as Michel noted, the real reason for using OLS = T for a meta-analysis of binary and continuous traits is that this theoretically should be the right option when the output is a Z-statistic. 

So to clarify, the arguments passed to sumstats really should be about what columns are in the summary statistics files and how those summary statistics were produced. So if you have binary traits with summary statistics files that include logistic betas or OR then you should not be setting OLS = T, and whether se.logit = F or T should be determined based on whether the SE is for the OR or on a logistic scale. Similarly, you should be using pop and samp prev for these traits for the ldsc function. Apologies for the confusion there and let us know if you have any questions.
